script.opening: (Slightly embarrassed, speaks quickly, a little breathless with nerves.) "This is going to sound silly — I keep getting these episodes where I can't catch my breath, my chest goes tight, my lips and fingers tingle and my heart races, and I feel like something awful's about to happen. I think it might be panic attacks… but a bit of me is terrified it's my heart or my lungs. Can you tell me it's not something serious?"

facts.text: "Usually when I'm stressed. They build up, then settle in about twenty minutes to half an hour. Afterwards I feel wiped out but normal." Two or three a week for 2 months. Hands sometimes cramp into a claw. Heart races but regular, she thinks.
"No, not with exercise. No wheeze that I've noticed." Runs twice a week without problems. No night cough. No childhood asthma.
"No blackouts. Not that I know of in the family" — no sudden deaths under 40 in the family, no chest pain on exertion.

"No, nothing like that" — no weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, heavy periods. "None of that" — no leg swelling, recent travel, surgery; not on the combined pill (has a copper coil); not pregnant.
"I've never really thought about it" — 4–5 coffees and two energy drinks a day. Doesn't smoke or vape, drinks at weekends, no drugs.
No regular medicines, no allergies. No previous anxiety diagnosis, though she was "a worrier" at university.

"There's a lot on at the moment, I suppose. I don't really want to get into it all today." If gently invited later: started a new job as a junior solicitor 3 months ago and split from her boyfriend. Sleeping badly. No low mood or thoughts of self-harm.
Can show the doctor her hands and breathing; has no pulse oximeter or BP machine.

Anxious but articulate. If the doctor says "it's just anxiety" without questions or tests, she feels dismissed: "That's what everyone says." Relieved when tests are offered: "That would put my mind at rest." Understands once the physiology is explained: "So the tingling is from the breathing? I thought it meant something awful." Prefers therapy to tablets.

ice.ideas: "Probably panic attacks — but maybe my heart or lungs."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "That I'll have a heart attack in one of them and nobody will take it seriously because I'm young." A new job and a break-up she doesn't want to discuss yet.
ice.expectations: "To be told it's not something serious — properly."

cues: "This is going to sound silly." — fear of being dismissed.
"Something awful's about to happen." — the sense of dread.
"A lot on at the moment." — stressors to return to gently.

checkpoints.text: Holds the principle that anxiety/panic/hyperventilation is a diagnosis of EXCLUSION — not labelling breathlessness as anxiety before excluding organic causes

Actively EXCLUDES organic causes relevant to a young adult — asthma (peak flow/spirometry), arrhythmia (palpitations/syncope/FAMILY HISTORY of sudden death; ECG), anaemia (FBC), hyperthyroidism (TFTs), PE if risk factors — with a focused examination arranged face to face (obs, sats, heart, chest, thyroid), as these cannot be done on video

Recognises the POSITIVE features of hyperventilation/panic (situational onset, peri-oral/peripheral tingling, carpopedal spasm, doom, rapid full recovery, normal exam) without using them to skip exclusion
Makes a POSITIVE diagnosis and EXPLAINS the physiology (over-breathing → low CO2 → tingling/light-headedness/chest tightness → more fear — a self-perpetuating cycle), destigmatising it

Manages anxiety/panic positively — breathing/relaxation techniques (not paper-bag), psychoeducation, CBT/psychological therapy (self-referral/NHS Talking Therapies), addressing triggers/stressors and lifestyle (caffeine/sleep), an SSRI licensed for panic disorder if preferred or significant (NICE CG113), no benzodiazepines — and screens mood/severity
Takes the fear (heart/lungs) seriously rather than dismissing, and lands reassurance on the back of genuine exclusion — a confident positive diagnosis, not "it’s just anxiety"
Explores any underlying stressor empathically, validates the distress, checks understanding, and supports engagement with psychological treatment

Safety-nets and follows up: which NEW/atypical features warrant review (exertional/positional symptoms, syncope, true wheeze, weight loss), results of any tests, the psychological-therapy plan and review — a positive diagnosis after exclusion, not a dismissive label

worked.txt: "It doesn’t sound silly at all — those episodes are genuinely frightening, and it’s sensible to want to be sure it’s not your heart or lungs. So rather than just say ‘it’s anxiety’, let me properly check the things that matter, and then we’ll know."

"A few questions: are you ever breathless or wheezy with exercise or at night? Any blackouts, or family members who died suddenly young? Any weight loss, tremor, feeling hot? … I can’t check your pulse, oxygen or listen to your chest over video, so I’d like you to come in so we can do that, with a heart tracing and some bloods — thyroid and blood count."

"Now — the tingling round your lips and in your fingers, the racing heart, the sense of dread, coming on with stress and settling in half an hour: those are very typical of panic and over-breathing, which is reassuring once we’ve checked the rest."

"Here’s what’s happening: when anxiety makes you breathe too fast, you blow off carbon dioxide, and that causes exactly these symptoms — tingling, light-headedness, tight chest. They feel alarming, which makes you breathe faster still. It’s a loop, not a heart attack — and that’s genuinely good news because we can break it."

"The most effective treatment is a talking therapy called CBT — you can refer yourself — plus some breathing techniques I’ll show you to use in the moment. Cutting caffeine and improving sleep help too. If the panic’s frequent and disabling, an SSRI antidepressant can also help — though not tranquillisers like diazepam, which aren’t recommended for panic."

"This is real and treatable, not ‘all in your head’. Once the tests are back I’ll confirm everything’s clear. But if you ever get breathless on exertion, blackout, or symptoms that don’t fit this pattern, come back — we’d look again. Is there anything stressful going on we should talk about?"

f.learning: Attributing breathlessness to ANXIETY/PANIC or HYPERVENTILATION must be a POSITIVE diagnosis made AFTER excluding organic causes — it is a diagnosis of EXCLUSION, never a lazy first label — and, even when the story sounds typically panic-like, genuine exclusion is both safer and more therapeutic, because a confident "I’ve checked and these are clear" reassures far better than a dismissive "it’s just anxiety". In a young adult, take a careful history and examination and exclude the relevant causes: ASTHMA (episodic/nocturnal/exertional wheeze, triggers, atopy — peak flow/spirometry ± FeNO), ARRHYTHMIA (palpitations, syncope/pre-syncope, exertional symptoms, family history of sudden cardiac death — ECG), ANAEMIA (FBC), HYPERTHYROIDISM (weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance — TFTs), PE (only if risk factors), and rarer cardiorespiratory disease, with focused examination arranged face to face (obs, sats, heart, chest, thyroid/anaemia signs — none of which can be done on video). Recognise the features that POSITIVELY fit hyperventilation/panic — situational/stress onset, peri-oral and peripheral tingling, carpopedal spasm, a sense of doom, light-headedness, rapid full recovery and a normal examination — without using them to skip exclusion. Then make a positive diagnosis and EXPLAIN the physiology in a destigmatising way: over-breathing lowers CO2, producing tingling, light-headedness and chest tightness, which feel frightening and drive more over-breathing — a self-perpetuating cycle, not a heart attack — because understanding the mechanism is itself therapeutic. Manage positively: controlled/diaphragmatic breathing techniques (not paper-bag), psychoeducation, CBT, an SSRI licensed for panic disorder or CBT-based self-help according to preference (NICE CG113; self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies), with no benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines or antipsychotics, addressing triggers/stressors and lifestyle (caffeine, sleep), screening mood and severity. Take the fear seriously, land reassurance on real exclusion, validate and treat the anxiety, and safety-net for new/atypical features.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG113 (generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults, 2011, updated 2020) · [2] NICE NG245 (asthma, 2024, joint with BTS and SIGN) · [3] NICE NG145 (thyroid disease, 2019) · [4] NICE NG158 (venous thromboembolic diseases, 2020, updated August 2023) · [5] NICE CG109 (transient loss of consciousness in over 16s, 2010) · [6] BNF
knowledge.summary: Episodic breathlessness with perioral and finger tingling, palpitations and dread at stressful times fits panic with over-breathing, but that label comes after a proportionate check for asthma, arrhythmia, anaemia, thyroid disease and, if risk factors, PE. Then make a confident positive diagnosis, explain the physiology, and offer CBT-based treatment.

points.t: Panic and hyperventilation should be diagnosed after the dangerous causes are reasonably excluded, and then stated confidently. Reassurance works when it rests on real checks the patient understands.

points.h: What to exclude in a young adult
points.t: Asthma: wheeze, night or exercise symptoms, atopy; NICE NG245 [2] starts objective testing in adults with blood eosinophils or FeNO, then spirometry with reversibility. Arrhythmia: palpitations with syncope, exertional symptoms or a family history of sudden cardiac death need an ECG and cardiology thinking (NICE CG109 [5] for blackouts). Hyperthyroidism: weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance; TFTs (NICE NG145 [3]). Anaemia: FBC. PE only if risk factors or pleuritic pain (NICE NG158 [4]).

Onset in stressful situations, perioral and finger tingling, carpopedal spasm, light-headedness, chest tightness, a sense of dread, and full recovery within 20 to 30 minutes, with normal findings between episodes. These support the diagnosis; they do not replace exclusion.

Over-breathing lowers carbon dioxide in the blood (respiratory alkalosis), causing tingling, light-headedness and chest tightness. Those sensations are frightening, so breathing speeds up further — a self-sustaining loop.

NICE CG113 [1] for panic disorder: offer CBT, an SSRI licensed for panic disorder, or CBT-based self-help, according to preference; NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral. Do not prescribe benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines or antipsychotics for panic disorder. Teach slow controlled breathing; paper-bag rebreathing is no longer advised.
Ask about frequency, avoidance, impact on work and life, low mood, alcohol and caffeine, and self-harm thoughts. A validated tool such as GAD-7 helps track response.
Re-assess if features change: breathlessness on exertion, chest pain on effort, blackouts, true wheeze, weight loss, or episodes that do not settle.

dg.d: Open question; let her finish; validated the fear rather than calling it silly.
Stress, caffeine, sleep and work; offered space to talk about what is going on.
Face-to-face obs, oxygen saturation, heart and chest exam, ECG, FBC and TFTs; asthma testing if features.
Panic with over-breathing versus asthma, arrhythmia, thyroid disease, anaemia and PE.
Asked about exertional symptoms, blackouts, family history of sudden death, weight loss, PE risk factors.
Positive diagnosis of panic with hyperventilation, explained physiologically, pending normal checks.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: CBT via NHS Talking Therapies, controlled breathing, caffeine reduction, SSRI as an option; no benzodiazepines (NICE CG113).
Sleep, caffeine and any stressor; mood and severity assessed.
Named triggers for re-assessment and 999; teach-back; results review in two weeks.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “terrified it’s my heart” and “nobody will take it seriously because I’m young”.
Idea (panic), concern (heart attack, not being believed), expectation (to be told it’s not serious).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "That I'll have a heart attack in one of them and nobody will take it seriously because I'm young." A new job and a break-up she doesn't want to discuss yet — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Hollie, I’m Dr Hughes. Tell me about these episodes — from the beginning.
model.why: Open question; lets her tell the story

model.text: This’ll sound silly. I get these episodes where I can’t catch my breath, my chest goes tight, my lips and fingers tingle, my heart races and I feel like something awful’s going to happen. I think it’s panic attacks, but part of me is terrified it’s my heart or lungs. Can you tell me it’s not serious?

It doesn’t sound silly at all — those episodes sound really frightening, and it’s sensible to want to be sure. I don’t want to just say “it’s anxiety”. I’d like to ask some questions, arrange some checks, and then explain what I think. Is that okay?
model.why: Validates the fear and sets a clear plan for the consultation

model.text: Yes, please.
When do they tend to happen, and how long do they last?
Usually when I’m stressed. They build up, then settle in about twenty minutes to half an hour. Afterwards I feel wiped out but normal.
Do they ever come on when you’re exercising or climbing stairs, or wake you from sleep? Any wheeze, or a cough at night?
No, not with exercise. No wheeze that I’ve noticed.
Have you ever blacked out or nearly blacked out? And has anyone in your family died suddenly at a young age, or had a heart rhythm problem?
model.why: Arrhythmia red flags and family history of sudden death

model.text: No blackouts. Not that I know of in the family.
Any weight loss, shakiness, feeling hot when others are cold, or heavier periods or tiredness recently?
No, nothing like that.
Any sharp pain on breathing in, calf swelling, recent long travel or surgery — and are you on any hormonal contraception?
None of that.
How much caffeine or alcohol do you have, and how’s your sleep?
I’ve never really thought about it.
You said part of you is terrified it’s your heart. What exactly worries you most?
That I’ll have a heart attack in one of them and nobody will take it seriously because I’m young.
That’s an important worry, and I am taking it seriously. How have things been for you generally — is there much going on at the moment?
model.why: Opens space for any stressor without assuming

model.text: There’s a lot on at the moment, I suppose. I don’t really want to get into it all today.
That’s fine. The door’s open whenever you want to.
model.why: Respects her pace while leaving the option open

model.text: I can’t examine you properly by video, so I’d like you to come in this week for your pulse, blood pressure, oxygen level, a listen to your heart and chest, a heart tracing, and blood tests for blood count and thyroid. If anything points to asthma, we’ll test for that too.
model.why: Arranges proportionate face-to-face examination and tests

model.text: Okay. That would put my mind at rest.

From what you’ve told me, the pattern fits panic attacks with over-breathing. When anxiety makes you breathe fast, you blow off carbon dioxide. That causes the tingling in your lips and fingers, the light-headedness and the tight chest. Those feelings are scary, so you breathe faster still. It’s a loop — not your heart failing.
model.why: Positive diagnosis with a physiological explanation

model.text: So the tingling is from the breathing? I thought it meant something awful.
Exactly — it’s a sign of over-breathing, not damage. Once the checks are back and normal, I’ll be able to say that with certainty.

The treatment that works best is a talking therapy called CBT, which teaches you to break the loop. You can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies. In the meantime, try slow breathing when an episode starts — gently in through your nose, then a longer, slower breath out. Keeping caffeine down and protecting your sleep help too. If the attacks are frequent and disabling, a daily medication called an SSRI is also an option.
model.why: NICE CG113 options; breathing technique; lifestyle

model.text: I’d rather try the therapy first.
That’s a good choice. I’ll send you the self-referral link. I also won’t be giving you tablets like diazepam — they aren’t recommended for panic and can cause dependence.
If you ever get breathless or chest pain when exercising, blackouts, a wheeze, or an episode that doesn’t settle and feels different, get seen. Severe chest pain that doesn’t settle — call 999.
Okay.
What will you take away from today?
Come in this week for the tests. It sounds like panic and over-breathing, not my heart. Self-refer for CBT, slow breathing, and watch the caffeine.
Perfect. I’ll go through the results with you in two weeks, and we can talk about anything else then if you want to.
model.why: Follow-up with results and open door

social.t: Panic often follows stress at work, study, relationships or money. Offer space to talk without forcing disclosure; she may return to it when trust is built.
If episodes affect work, a fit note can suggest adjustments, such as phased duties, rather than time off.

legal.t: DVLA: anxiety needs notifying only if it affects safe driving (for example through poor concentration or agitation); any loss of consciousness would change the advice.

professional.t: Young women with breathlessness and chest symptoms are at risk of having organic disease attributed to anxiety. Document the exclusion process and the safety-net.
NICE CG113 and BNF guidance: avoid benzodiazepines in panic disorder because of dependence and poorer long-term outcomes.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies self-referral, NHS Every Mind Matters, and the charity Anxiety UK.

redFlags: Breathlessness or chest pain on exertion
Syncope or pre-syncope, or family history of sudden cardiac death
Wheeze, night cough, weight loss, tremor or heat intolerance
Pleuritic pain, calf swelling or VTE risk factors
psychosocial: Current stressors, when she is ready
Impact on work and avoidance of situations
ice: Concern: “What if it’s my heart and nobody believes me because I’m young?”
Expectation: to be told it isn’t serious

playbook.diagnosis: “The pattern fits panic attacks with over-breathing. I’ll confirm that with an examination, a heart tracing and blood tests this week.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “When you breathe too fast you blow off carbon dioxide, and that causes the tingling, light-headedness and tight chest. They feel scary, so you breathe faster still. It’s a loop we can learn to break.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried nobody would take this seriously because you’re young. I have, and the checks are part of that.”
management.psychosocial: Invite, don’t push, discussion of stressors; cut caffeine; improve sleep; support her preference for therapy first.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face obs, oxygen saturation, examination and ECG; FBC and TFTs
CBT via NHS Talking Therapies self-referral (NICE CG113); SSRI if she prefers or if severe; no benzodiazepines
Slow controlled breathing technique; less caffeine
safetyNet: Get seen for exertional breathlessness or chest pain, blackouts, wheeze, or episodes that feel different
999 for severe chest pain that doesn’t settle

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost at both ends: by labelling anxiety too early, or by investigating so broadly that the panic is never named or treated. The marks are in a focused exclusion followed by a confident, explained diagnosis.

items.fail: “This sounds like anxiety” in the first two minutes, with no exclusion questions.
items.why: “Fails to consider serious alternative diagnoses.” Arrhythmia and asthma can present exactly like this.
items.fix: Ask the exertion, blackout, family history, thyroid and PE questions out loud.

items.fail: Saying “I’ll listen to your chest and check your oxygen” during a video consultation.
items.why: You cannot examine by video; claiming to do so is unsafe and inaccurate.
items.fix: Arrange a face-to-face examination with ECG and bloods this week.

items.fail: Ordering tests but never naming panic or offering treatment.
items.why: Leaves her frightened and still having attacks; no positive diagnosis earns no management marks.
items.fix: Name the likely diagnosis, explain the carbon dioxide loop, offer CBT today.

items.fail: Missing “nobody will take it seriously because I’m young”.
items.why: That is her real concern; ignoring it undermines every reassurance that follows.
items.fix: Answer it directly: “I am taking it seriously — that’s why we’re checking.”

items.why: NICE CG113 advises against benzodiazepines in panic disorder.
items.fix: CBT first, SSRI if needed, breathing technique for the moment.

items.why: A positive diagnosis still needs criteria for re-assessment.
items.fix: Name exertional symptoms, blackouts, wheeze and different episodes; book a results review.

timeMap.d: Let her describe an episode fully; tell her the fear is reasonable.
Pattern and duration; exertion, wheeze, blackouts, family history of sudden death, thyroid, anaemia, PE risk; caffeine and sleep.
Fear of a heart attack and of not being believed; space for any stressor.
Face-to-face exam, ECG, FBC, TFTs. Explain over-breathing and the loop.
CBT self-referral, breathing, caffeine, SSRI option, no benzodiazepines, safety-net, teach-back, results review.

wordPics.fail: Labels it “just anxiety” within two minutes; no questions about exertion, blackouts or family history; no checks; or the opposite — a long list of tests with no explanation and no treatment for the panic.
wordPics.pass: Screens the important organic causes, arranges exam, ECG and bloods, explains panic with over-breathing, and offers CBT with a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains the carbon dioxide loop in plain words so the tingling stops being frightening; links reassurance to the checks; addresses her fear of not being believed; offers CBT, breathing and caffeine advice in line with NICE CG113; avoids benzodiazepines; follows up with results.

avoid.dont: “It’s just anxiety, you’re young and healthy.”
avoid.instead: “The pattern fits panic, and I’d like to check a few things so we can both be sure.”
avoid.why: Premature labelling feels dismissive and is unsafe.

avoid.dont: “Breathe into a paper bag when it happens.”
avoid.instead: “Breathe slowly — in through your nose, and a longer breath out.”
avoid.why: Paper-bag rebreathing is no longer advised.

avoid.dont: “I’ll give you some diazepam for the attacks.”
avoid.instead: “The best treatment is CBT, and there’s a daily medicine if you need it.”
avoid.why: NICE CG113 advises against benzodiazepines for panic disorder.

SCA_STEM.recent: Booked video consultation: recurrent episodes of breathlessness.
SCA_STEM.reason: “I keep getting breathless and tingly — I think it’s panic, but what if it’s my heart?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG113 (generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults, 2011, updated 2020) · [2] NICE NG245 (asthma, 2024, joint with BTS and SIGN) · [3] NICE NG145 (thyroid disease, 2019) · [4] NICE NG158 (venous thromboembolic diseases, 2020, updated August 2023) · [5] NICE CG109 (transient loss of consciousness in over 16s, 2010) · [6] BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Episodic breathlessness with perioral and finger tingling, palpitations and dread at stressful times fits panic with over-breathing, but that label comes after a proportionate check for asthma, arrhythmia, anaemia, thyroid disease and, if risk factors, PE. Then make a confident positive diagnosis, explain the physiology, and offer CBT-based treatment.

points.t: Panic and hyperventilation should be diagnosed after the dangerous causes are reasonably excluded, and then stated confidently. Reassurance works when it rests on real checks the patient understands.

points.h: What to exclude in a young adult
points.t: Asthma: wheeze, night or exercise symptoms, atopy; NICE NG245 [2] starts objective testing in adults with blood eosinophils or FeNO, then spirometry with reversibility. Arrhythmia: palpitations with syncope, exertional symptoms or a family history of sudden cardiac death need an ECG and cardiology thinking (NICE CG109 [5] for blackouts). Hyperthyroidism: weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance; TFTs (NICE NG145 [3]). Anaemia: FBC. PE only if risk factors or pleuritic pain (NICE NG158 [4]).

Onset in stressful situations, perioral and finger tingling, carpopedal spasm, light-headedness, chest tightness, a sense of dread, and full recovery within 20 to 30 minutes, with normal findings between episodes. These support the diagnosis; they do not replace exclusion.

Over-breathing lowers carbon dioxide in the blood (respiratory alkalosis), causing tingling, light-headedness and chest tightness. Those sensations are frightening, so breathing speeds up further — a self-sustaining loop.

NICE CG113 [1] for panic disorder: offer CBT, an SSRI licensed for panic disorder, or CBT-based self-help, according to preference; NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral. Do not prescribe benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines or antipsychotics for panic disorder. Teach slow controlled breathing; paper-bag rebreathing is no longer advised.
Ask about frequency, avoidance, impact on work and life, low mood, alcohol and caffeine, and self-harm thoughts. A validated tool such as GAD-7 helps track response.
Re-assess if features change: breathlessness on exertion, chest pain on effort, blackouts, true wheeze, weight loss, or episodes that do not settle.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her finish; validated the fear rather than calling it silly.
Stress, caffeine, sleep and work; offered space to talk about what is going on.
Picked up “terrified it’s my heart” and “nobody will take it seriously because I’m young”.
Idea (panic), concern (heart attack, not being believed), expectation (to be told it’s not serious).
Face-to-face obs, oxygen saturation, heart and chest exam, ECG, FBC and TFTs; asthma testing if features.
Panic with over-breathing versus asthma, arrhythmia, thyroid disease, anaemia and PE.
Asked about exertional symptoms, blackouts, family history of sudden death, weight loss, PE risk factors.
Positive diagnosis of panic with hyperventilation, explained physiologically, pending normal checks.
CBT via NHS Talking Therapies, controlled breathing, caffeine reduction, SSRI as an option; no benzodiazepines (NICE CG113).
Sleep, caffeine and any stressor; mood and severity assessed.
Named triggers for re-assessment and 999; teach-back; results review in two weeks.

social.t: Panic often follows stress at work, study, relationships or money. Offer space to talk without forcing disclosure; she may return to it when trust is built.
If episodes affect work, a fit note can suggest adjustments, such as phased duties, rather than time off.

legal.t: DVLA: anxiety needs notifying only if it affects safe driving (for example through poor concentration or agitation); any loss of consciousness would change the advice.

professional.t: Young women with breathlessness and chest symptoms are at risk of having organic disease attributed to anxiety. Document the exclusion process and the safety-net.
NICE CG113 and BNF guidance: avoid benzodiazepines in panic disorder because of dependence and poorer long-term outcomes.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies self-referral, NHS Every Mind Matters, and the charity Anxiety UK.

redFlags: Breathlessness or chest pain on exertion
Syncope or pre-syncope, or family history of sudden cardiac death
Wheeze, night cough, weight loss, tremor or heat intolerance
Pleuritic pain, calf swelling or VTE risk factors
psychosocial: Current stressors, when she is ready
Impact on work and avoidance of situations
ice: Concern: “What if it’s my heart and nobody believes me because I’m young?”
Expectation: to be told it isn’t serious

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The pattern fits panic attacks with over-breathing. I’ll confirm that with an examination, a heart tracing and blood tests this week.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “When you breathe too fast you blow off carbon dioxide, and that causes the tingling, light-headedness and tight chest. They feel scary, so you breathe faster still. It’s a loop we can learn to break.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried nobody would take this seriously because you’re young. I have, and the checks are part of that.”
management.psychosocial: Invite, don’t push, discussion of stressors; cut caffeine; improve sleep; support her preference for therapy first.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face obs, oxygen saturation, examination and ECG; FBC and TFTs
CBT via NHS Talking Therapies self-referral (NICE CG113); SSRI if she prefers or if severe; no benzodiazepines
Slow controlled breathing technique; less caffeine
safetyNet: Get seen for exertional breathlessness or chest pain, blackouts, wheeze, or episodes that feel different
999 for severe chest pain that doesn’t settle

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost at both ends: by labelling anxiety too early, or by investigating so broadly that the panic is never named or treated. The marks are in a focused exclusion followed by a confident, explained diagnosis.

items.fail: “This sounds like anxiety” in the first two minutes, with no exclusion questions.
items.why: “Fails to consider serious alternative diagnoses.” Arrhythmia and asthma can present exactly like this.
items.fix: Ask the exertion, blackout, family history, thyroid and PE questions out loud.

items.fail: Saying “I’ll listen to your chest and check your oxygen” during a video consultation.
items.why: You cannot examine by video; claiming to do so is unsafe and inaccurate.
items.fix: Arrange a face-to-face examination with ECG and bloods this week.

items.fail: Ordering tests but never naming panic or offering treatment.
items.why: Leaves her frightened and still having attacks; no positive diagnosis earns no management marks.
items.fix: Name the likely diagnosis, explain the carbon dioxide loop, offer CBT today.

items.fail: Missing “nobody will take it seriously because I’m young”.
items.why: That is her real concern; ignoring it undermines every reassurance that follows.
items.fix: Answer it directly: “I am taking it seriously — that’s why we’re checking.”

items.why: NICE CG113 advises against benzodiazepines in panic disorder.
items.fix: CBT first, SSRI if needed, breathing technique for the moment.

items.why: A positive diagnosis still needs criteria for re-assessment.
items.fix: Name exertional symptoms, blackouts, wheeze and different episodes; book a results review.
